inline.s: (Mengyou ji: "Instruction to Student Ou Boyu")
Diligence and hard work, correct method, and unflagging perseverance.
Heaven does not fail the person who truly strives.

It has been said that all sages and ordinary beings, without exception, accomplish their worldly and world-transcending undertakings through aspiration and resolve. From this we know that one who aspires to the nature and the wisdom-life aspires to leave birth and death, while one who aspires to merit, fame, wealth, and honor aspires to enter birth and death.

The ancient worthies said: "All sages and ordinary beings, without exception, accomplish their worldly and world-transcending undertakings through aspiration and resolve." From this we know that one who aspires to the Dharma-body and the wisdom-life aspires to leave birth and death (attaining outstanding achievement in the realization of the Dharma-body); one who aspires to merit, fame, wealth, and honor aspires to enter birth and death (attaining outstanding achievement in the illusory arena of birth and death).
[nature and wisdom-life] the inherent nature and the wisdom-life of living beings, that is, the Dharma-body and the wisdom-life.

My teacher said: "The vast sea of wisdom has been turned into the sea of karma that is birth and death; the precious, bright, wondrous nature has been obscured into the karma-nature of greed, anger, folly, and pride, which is birth and death." Seen from this, the source of the true and the false is already not two in our nature; if one knows how to enter birth and death through greed, anger, and folly, then one can also use greed, anger, and folly to leave birth and death.

My teacher said: "The vast sea of wisdom, through delusion, becomes the sea of karma that is birth and death; the precious, bright, wondrous nature, through obscuration, becomes the karma-nature of greed, anger, folly, and pride, which is birth and death." Seen from this, since the source of the true and the false is one and the same (when the self-nature is deluded, one is an ordinary being; when the self-nature is awakened, one is a Buddha), if one knows how to obtain merit, fame, wealth, and honor through greed, anger, and folly, then one can know how to make use of greed, anger, and folly to leave the cycle of birth and death.

[if one knows how to enter birth and death through greed, anger, and folly, one can also use greed, anger, and folly to leave birth and death] Accomplishing cultivation and accomplishing fame and fortune both require diligence and hard work, a correct method, and unflagging perseverance. Therefore it is said that if one knows how to obtain merit, fame, wealth, and honor through greed, anger, and folly, one can know how to make use of greed, anger, and folly to leave the cycle of birth and death. Layman Pang said: "The ten directions gather together, each one studying the unconditioned; this is the place for selecting Buddhas — empty the mind and return having passed the examination." [passing the examination] passing the imperial examination to become a jinshi; in the Ming and Qing dynasties this was used only for the top three of the palace examination: zhuangyuan, bangyan, and tanhua. [hard work] being able to persist through dull, tedious, and arduous training of great volume. "The edge of a treasured sword comes from whetting; the fragrance of plum blossom comes from bitter cold." Life requires tempering; one must continually challenge and surpass oneself. [correct method] This point is very important. If the method is wrong, the ancient worthies described it thus: grinding a brick cannot make a mirror. [one can also use greed, anger, and folly to leave birth and death] This is dispelling illusion with illusion; when illusion is exhausted, the true appears.

There is a proverb: "He whose hatred is small is no true gentleman; he who has no venom is no true man." In my daily life I often reflect: Goujian, because of the shame of Kuaiji, resolved to avenge himself upon Wu, and so he slept on brushwood and tasted gall for more than twenty years, wearing no fine garments and eating no rich food, until at last he destroyed Wu and became hegemon.

The proverb says: "He whose hatred is small is no true gentleman; he who has no venom is no true man." In my daily life I often reflect: Goujian, because of the shame of Kuaiji, resolved to destroy Wu and avenge himself, and so he slept on brushwood and tasted gall for more than twenty years, wearing coarse clothes and eating plain food, until at last he destroyed Wu and became hegemon over the realm.
[sleeping on brushwood and tasting gall] The Records of the Grand Historian,

"The Hereditary House of Goujian, King of Yue," records: "When Goujian, King of Yue, returned to his state, he afflicted his body and anxiously pondered, placing a gall bladder where he sat; whether sitting or lying he looked up at the gall, and when eating or drinking he tasted the gall." [double-

The story of sleeping on brushwood and tasting gall:

King Fuchai of Wu, in order to avenge his father, led his troops to attack the state of Yue. Goujian's forces of several tens of thousands were wiped out, and in the end only five thousand men remained, surrounded by the great army of Wu at Kuaiji. With no way out, Goujian prepared to kill himself. At this point his advisor Wen Zhong stopped him, saying: "The Wu minister Bo Pi is greedy for wealth and lustful; we can send someone to bribe him." Goujian followed Wen Zhong's suggestion and sent him with treasures to bribe Bo Pi, and Bo Pi agreed to go with Wen Zhong to see the King of Wu. Wen Zhong saw the King of Wu, presented the treasures, and said: "The King of Yue is willing to surrender and become your servant to wait upon you; please spare him." Bo Pi also spoke up in support of Wen Zhong. Wu Zixu stepped forward and loudly objected: "People often say: 'To cure an illness, remove its root.' Goujian is far-sighted and deep in his planning, and Wen Zhong and Fan Li are shrewd and capable. If we let them go this time, once they return they will find a way to take revenge!" At this time Fuchai believed that Yue was no longer a threat, and so he did not heed Wu Zixu's counsel. He accepted Yue's surrender and withdrew his army back to Wu.

After the Wu troops withdrew, Goujian went to Wu with his wife and the minister Fan Li to wait upon the King of Wu. In order to humiliate Goujian, the King of Wu sent him to tend the tombs and feed the horses. Although the King of Yue was furious within, he still did his utmost to appear loyal and submissive. When the King of Wu went out, he walked in front respectfully leading the horse; when the King of Wu was ill, he attended him diligently at his bedside, so as to win the King of Wu's favor and trust. Seeing how wholeheartedly he served him, the King of Wu felt that he was extremely loyal, and after three years allowed him to return to Yue.

After returning to his state, Goujian resolved to strengthen himself and prepare for revenge. Fearing that he would become attached to a comfortable life and let his will for vengeance wear away, at night he pillowed his head on weapons and slept on a pile of brushwood. In order never to forget revenge and the recovery of his state, he hung a bitter gall bladder in his room, and before sitting down, lying down, and eating, he would lick and taste it. When he passed in or out of the room, the soldiers outside the door would ask him: "Have you forgotten the shame of three years?" He sent Wen Zhong to administer the affairs of state and Fan Li to manage the military, while he himself went into the fields to work alongside the farmers, and his wife spun and wove like the common women. He treated the wise and able with the utmost respect, gave rich gifts to his guests, aided the poor, and mourned the dead. These actions of Goujian moved the officials and people of Yue. Thus, with the whole state of one mind, after ten years of accumulating and ten years of instruction, Yue at last became rich in people and strong in state, with fine troops and ample provisions.
[ten years of accumulating and ten years of instruction] accumulating: increasing the population and amassing resources; instruction: educating the people and training the army.

Meanwhile, King Fuchai of Wu blindly strove for hegemony, giving not the slightest thought to the people's hardships. He also heeded the slander of Bo Pi and killed his loyal minister Wu Zixu. In the end Fuchai succeeded in his bid for hegemony and became leader over the feudal lords. But the Wu of this time, though seemingly powerful, was in fact already in decline.
In

BC, Fuchai personally led a great army north to contend with the state of Jin for leadership of the feudal lords. King Goujian of Yue, taking advantage of the fact that Wu's elite troops were abroad, launched a surprise attack, defeated the Wu army at a single stroke, and killed Crown Prince You. When Fuchai heard the news, he hurried back with his troops and sent envoys to sue for peace with Goujian. Goujian reckoned that he could not destroy Wu all at once, and agreed. Nine years later, in

BC, Goujian personally led his troops a second time to attack Wu. By this time Wu was a spent force, utterly unable to withstand the fierce assault of the Yue army, and was defeated in battle after battle. In the end Fuchai again sent envoys to sue for peace, but Fan Li firmly insisted on destroying Wu. Seeing that peace was not to be had, Fuchai regretted that he had not heeded Wu Zixu's loyal counsel, and, overcome with shame, drew his sword and killed himself.

We students of the Way: consider the birth and death of successive kalpas, our imprisonment and humiliation in the prison of the three realms — is this not far greater than the shame of Kuaiji? Greed, anger, folly, and pride rob the light of our wondrous nature and break down the house of our nirvana — is this not far greater than the enmity of Wu? Yet we are contented as if eating sweet syrup, sporting and feasting among them, with not the slightest sense of shame or of rousing hatred. This can truly be called a great ignorance of the root! If we look at ourselves, can we be called great heroes? Boyu, since you aspire to this, you should gnash your teeth over it!

We students of the Way, let us compare and examine: the birth and death of successive kalpas, our imprisonment and humiliation in the prison of the three realms — is this not far more than the shame of Kuaiji? Greed, anger, folly, and pride rob the light of our wondrous nature and break down the house of our nirvana — is this not far more than the enmity of Wu? Yet we are contented as if eating sweet syrup, sporting and feasting among them, with not the slightest sense of shame or of rousing hatred. This can truly be called a great ignorance of the root! We may examine ourselves: can such as this be called a great hero? Boyu, since you aspire to the Dharma-body and the wisdom-life, you should gnash your teeth and rouse your resolve over this!

[the three realms] the realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm. The realm of desire is the world inhabited by beings who have the two desires of lust and food: above, the six heavens of desire; in the middle, the four great continents inhabited by humans and animals; below, down to the Unintermittent Hell — all belong to it. The realm of form is the world inhabited by beings without the two desires of lust and food but who still have form: the eighteen heavens of the four dhyanas all belong to it. The formless realm is the world inhabited by beings who have no form at all but who dwell in mind-consciousness within profound, wondrous samadhi: the four heavens of emptiness belong to it. These three realms are all the realms in which ordinary beings pass through birth and death, and so the practitioner of the Buddha's way takes leaving the three realms as the goal. [contented as if eating sweet syrup] as joyful as eating sugar. [sporting and feasting] playing and banqueting.
